summary: Defines a DHCP option for IPv4 that lets iSNS clients discover the iSNS server automatically. iSNS provides discovery and management for iSCSI and iFCP storage devices. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: When you join a network, a helper tells you where the directory desk is. This memo adds a line to that helper's message for finding the storage directory.

questions: how to find isns server automatically
how do clients find an isns server
what does the isns dhcp option contain
subtitle: A DHCP option, number 83, that tells storage devices where to find their iSNS server and how to use it.

tldr.problem: iSCSI and iFCP devices need to find their iSNS server, and no existing DHCP option can carry both its location and which iSNS services the client may use.
tldr.mechanism: DHCP option 83 carries bit fields for functions, Discovery Domain access, administrative flags and server security, followed by the IP addresses of the primary and backup iSNS servers.
tldr.outcome: Storage devices can learn where the iSNS server is and how it is configured straight from DHCP, though the option is only as trustworthy as the DHCP exchange unless IPsec or DHCP authentication is used.

today: RFC 4174 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7146. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a New DHCP Option
sections.content:
DHCP for IPv4 passes configuration to hosts, including devices that reach block storage over TCP/IP using iSCSI and iFCP. The iSNS protocol provides automated discovery, management and configuration of those devices, giving IP networks storage intelligence comparable to what Fibre Channel networks have.

The RFC argues that existing DHCP options cannot find iSNS servers. iSNS does much more than a name-resolution protocol such as DNS, and the option must say not just where the server is but which subset of iSNS services the client may use. The DHCP option number assigned for iSNS is 83.
sections.plainLanguage: The old messages from the network helper had no room for this. So a new line was added that says where the directory desk is and what it can do.

sections.title: The iSNS Option Layout
sections.content:
The option holds the location of the primary and backup iSNS servers and the services available to the client. After the Code (83) and Length octets come four fields: iSNS Functions, Discovery Domain Access, Administrative Flags and the iSNS Server Security Bitmap. Then come IP addresses a1...a4, optionally b1...b4, and any additional secondary servers, four octets each.

Length counts the bytes that follow it. The fields through a1...a4 MUST be present in every response, so the minimum Length is 14. If the Heartbeat bit is set, b1...b4 MUST also be present and the minimum is 18. Extra secondary servers are indicated by increasing Length. Formats use big-endian byte order and RESERVED bits SHOULD be zero.

What a1...a4 holds depends on the Heartbeat bit. If set, it is the multicast address for iSNS heartbeat messages, and b1...b4 is the primary server. If clear, a1...a4 is the primary server itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a short form with a few checkbox rows, followed by a list of addresses. The first address is the main desk, and any more are spares.

sections.title: Functions and Discovery Domain Access
sections.content:
The iSNS Functions field says how the server is to be used, from simple discovery up to distributing IKE/IPsec security policies and certificates. Its bits are Function Fields Enabled (bit 15), DD-Based Authorization (14) and Security Policy Distribution (13). If the enabled bit is zero, the other function bits MUST be ignored.

DD-Based Authorization says whether devices in a common Discovery Domain (DD) may access each other automatically, if authenticated. Devices not sharing a domain are never allowed to access each other. Security Policy Distribution says whether the client must use the security policy stored on the iSNS server.

The DD Access field has an Enabled bit, a Control Node bit (whether Control Nodes may add, modify or delete Discovery Domains), and four bits for iSCSI Target, iSCSI Initiator, iFCP Target Port and iFCP Initiator Port, saying which client types may modify domains. A node may implement several types.
sections.plainLanguage: These checkboxes say which rooms devices are allowed to peek into, and who is allowed to move devices between rooms.

sections.title: Administrative Flags and Security Bitmap
sections.content:
The Administrative Flags field has an Enabled bit (15, and if zero, the rest MUST be ignored because settings come from elsewhere), Heartbeat (14), Management SCNs (13) and Default Discovery Domain (12). Management SCNs are State Change Notifications whose scope is the whole iSNS database, and the bit says whether control nodes may register for them. The Default Discovery Domain bit says whether devices not placed in any DD are automatically put in a default DD.

The iSNS Server Security Bitmap tells the client which security settings are needed to talk to the server. Its bits are Enabled (31), IKE/IPSec (30), Main Mode (29), Aggressive Mode (28), PFS (27), Transport Mode (26) and Tunnel Mode (25). If IKE/IPsec is disabled, other key exchange such as manual keying can still be used. If enabled, exactly one of Main Mode and Aggressive Mode MUST be set, and exactly one of Transport Mode and Tunnel Mode MUST be set.
sections.plainLanguage: More checkboxes say whether the server sends regular hello pings, whether new devices get a default room, and what kind of secret handshake the server wants.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DHCP authentication may be a poor fit because it has seen limited implementation and deployment. IPsec for iSNS itself is specified in the iSNS document, and an authentication block protects multicast and broadcast heartbeat and discovery messages.

Without DHCP security, false discovery information is a risk, for example an option pointing at a fake iSNS server. The main countermeasure is authentication by the storage protocols that are discovered, and where the risk matters, IPsec security associations SHOULD be used, including for iSNS traffic.

When IPsec is implemented, false information could trigger repeated IKE negotiation as a denial-of-service attack. When this DHCP option is used, iSNS entities MUST implement three measures: limiting peers by IP address range, limiting peers by DNS domain, and keeping a negative authentication cache.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could give a computer the address of a fake directory. So devices should check who they are really talking to, and avoid wasting time on peers that already failed the check.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the value 83 for this option under the policy defined in the DHCP specification. This document defines no other IANA-assigned values.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers gave this option the number 83. Nothing else on that list changed.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Bytes that follow the Length field.

fields.name: DD Access
fields.desc: Which client types may modify Discovery Domains.

fields.name: iSNS Server Security Bitmap
fields.desc: Security settings needed to reach the server.

fields.name: a1 a2 a3 a4
fields.desc: Heartbeat origin or primary server address.
